First, I’m a kid. Then there’s Type 1 Diabetes.

I’m Aviva. I’m a Youth Ambassador for Breakthrough T1D because I enjoy helping my community. I like to give back through food security initiatives at Ampowering, by walking runways to raise disability awareness, or helping elementary kids find their buses on Safety Patrol. I also live with Type 1 Diabetes. This means that my days come with extra data, glucose checks, alarms and balancing, but it has never been the whole story. This is my site for raising awareness and funds for T1D research.

About Aviva

A student, an advocate, and a kid first

My story starts with the things I love doing. Type 1 Diabetes is part of it, an important part, but it comes second.

Who I am

I’m a student who loves karate, music, school, runways, and advocacy. Yes, with Type 1 diabetes, it was initially difficult to continue some of the things I loved like the swim team, karate or modeling. But with the support of my teachers and mentors I found a way to make the math and magic work! That means you can too.

My T1D story

I was diagnosed with Type 1 Diabetes just a few days after my 7th birthday. When I went back to school, things felt different. I was not invited to sleepovers or parties, and all the kids wanted to know what the “patch” on my arm was. Rather than being sad, I chose to stay positive and educate everyone around me.

Why I speak up

I created Aviva Cares to demystify T1D for classmates and teachers, raise funds for a cure through Breakthrough T1D, and turn my journey into action for others. My diagnosis became a starting point for speaking up and ensuring that no one with a disability feels lonely or left out.

“When you live with Type 1 Diabetes, every single day is a science experiment… it just means living life with extra data and a lot of resilience.”

From T1D 101 for Schools & Friends

My diaversary is a celebration

Every year, we mark my diaversary, the anniversary of my diagnosis, not as a sad date, but as a celebration: another year of doing hard things, learning my body, and living without limits. Resilience is worth celebrating.

Research

Research runs in my family

Science improves the technology that helps people keep track of our bodies every day. AvivaCares partners with ImagineQ Labs to publish research on biosignals, and how they can be used to detect stress, burn-out, or even hypoglycemia (low blood sugar).

Conference paper · ICSIPA 2026

Electrodermal Activity as a Unimodal Signal for Aerobic Exercise Detection in Wearable Sensors

Rena Mira Krishna, Ramya Sankar, Shadi Ghiasi

Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE 9th International Conference on Signal & Image Processing Applications (ICSIPA 2026), September 9, 2026, Melaka, Malaysia. First published March 2026 as arXiv:2603.15880 · DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2603.15880

What the paper is about

Electrodermal activity (EDA) is a signal many wearables can already measure without any extra hardware. It reflects how the sympathetic nervous system responds, for instance when the body starts working hard. This study asks a focused question: can features from EDA alone reliably tell rest apart from sustained aerobic exercise? To find out, the team used data from thirty healthy individuals and tested benchmark machine learning models with leave-one-subject-out validation, so every model was judged on people it had never seen. The EDA-only classifiers reached moderate subject-independent performance, and the timing and shape of the signal’s fast-changing phasic component helped most in separating the two states. The authors are careful about the limits: the paper is a conservative benchmark of what EDA on its own can do, not a replacement for wearables that combine several signals.

Personal Story & Mission September 2025

All About My Type 1 Diabetes

Hi! I’m Aviva. I enjoy zip-lining, traveling, singing, and reading about superheroes. I have Type 1 Diabetes. My body is awesome, but it needs a little help.

I have Type 1 Diabetes

  • Type 1 Diabetes means that my pancreas doesn’t make insulin.
  • Insulin is like a “key” that allows sugar to enter cells.
  • Without insulin, my body cannot use the carbs and sugar in food to give me energy. Instead, the sugar stays in my blood and makes me tired.
  • So I take insulin as a medicine to stay healthy and play!
  • Type 1 Diabetes is not contagious. You cannot catch it like the flu.

Math helps me manage my blood sugars

Blood sugar is how much sugar is in our blood from the food we eat. I use math to “think like a pancreas” and keep it just right!

  • When it’s too low: I feel shaky, sweaty, or dizzy. I eat a quick snack like juice or candy to fix it! It’s a treat — it’s also like medicine for me.
  • When it’s too high: I feel thirsty or tired. I give myself insulin to feel OK and drink more water. Don’t worry, it’s easy and I know how to handle it!

Technology helps me manage my T1D

  • I check my blood sugar with a sensor. You’ll see a patch on my arm.
  • My sensor connects to my watch, which alerts me when I’m high or low.
  • I wear a Pod on my legs that gives me insulin. I use a phone-like device, a “PDM,” to manage the Pod.
  • These devices work together to help me think like a pancreas!
  • They don’t hurt much. I like to think I’m a superhero like Iron Man or Cyborg!

Lots of famous people have T1D

We are just like you. Lots of famous people live with Type 1 Diabetes too:

  • Wasim Akram — cricketer
  • Lila Moss — supermodel
  • Bambi Blyth — supermodel
  • Nick Jonas — singer
  • Sonia Sotomayor — Associate Justice of the United States
  • Alexander Zverev — tennis player
  • Theresa May — former UK Prime Minister
  • JJ Spaun — golfer and US Open winner
  • Katie Bone — rock climber
  • Gary Hall — swimmer with 5 Olympic gold medals (10 medals in total)
  • Nacho Fernandez — soccer player
  • Ed Gamble — comedian
  • Hermona Girmay — Ms Washington ’25
  • Brynn Lansford — first officer
  • Chad Muma — NFL player
  • Logan Brown — NFL player

Thank you for listening!

  • Don’t worry if you hear my pump or Pod beep or make sounds — it alerts me to have a snack.
  • Sometimes I check my sugar or eat a snack in class when I feel dizzy.
  • I can help you with Algebra. I use it daily.
  • Any questions?

School Advocacy & Peer Awareness September 2024

What That Beep Means — A Guide to CGM Alarms in the Classroom

If you hear a high-pitched tune or a repeated buzz from my desk or backpack, don’t worry — I’m not playing a game on my phone! That sound comes from my Continuous Glucose Monitor (CGM). It measures my blood sugar continuously and alerts me if my levels are going too high or dropping low.

  • High Alarms: Means my body needs extra water or an insulin adjustment.
  • Low Alarms: Means I need quick-acting sugar immediately (like juice boxes or fruit gummies).
  • How classmates can help: You don’t need to panic! Just let the teacher know if I look tired or shaky, and give me a minute to treat my low.

What the different beeps mean

My CGM checks my blood sugar all the time, and the beep is how it gets my attention. There are two alarms you are most likely to hear in class:

  • The high alarm: My blood sugar is going too high. It means my body needs extra water or an insulin adjustment. When I hear it, I check my numbers and follow my care plan.
  • The low alarm: My blood sugar is dropping low. It means I need quick-acting sugar immediately, like juice boxes or fruit gummies. This is the alarm I act on right away.

Either way, the beep is the monitor doing its job — it is telling me something so I can take care of it.

When the alarm says my blood sugar is low

A low alarm is the one to act on right away. Here is what I do, and what helps me:

  • I follow my care plan.
  • I have fast-acting sugar right away — juice boxes or fruit gummies are my go-tos.
  • I tell an adult, like my teacher, so a grown-up knows what is happening.
  • I recheck my blood sugar to make sure it is coming back up.

And here is how classmates can help:

  1. Do not panic. The beep is the monitor doing its job.
  2. Let the teacher know if I look tired or shaky.
  3. Give me a minute to treat my low.

T1D Education June 2024

Type 1 vs. Type 2 Diabetes — Busting the Biggest Myths

One of the most common things people ask is: “Did you get diabetes from eating too many sweets?” The short answer is: No.

  1. Type 1 Diabetes (T1D): An autoimmune condition where the body’s immune system accidentally attacks the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. Nothing I ate or did caused it, and it cannot be cured by diet or exercise.
  2. Type 2 Diabetes: A metabolic condition where the body becomes resistant to insulin or doesn’t produce enough.

Understanding the difference helps eliminate stigma and ensures kids with T1D get the exact medical support and understanding they need at school and sports.

How a healthy cell works

  • You eat or drink, food breaks down into glucose.
  • The pancreas makes insulin from beta cells.
  • Insulin is the key and it turns easily.
  • The door opens and glucose goes in.
  • The cell makes energy.

Healthy result: insulin is made, the key turns easily, the door opens, and glucose becomes energy, not a pile-up in the blood.

Gestational diabetes

Gestational diabetes only develops during pregnancy. It is not Type 1 and it is not Type 2.

  • Pancreas still works, beta cells still make insulin and keys.
  • Placenta hormones make the key difficult to turn.
  • The cell door opens less, so blood sugar rises in pregnancy.

What happens: hormones from the placenta make the mother’s insulin harder to use, a temporary form of insulin resistance, a bit like the stuck lock in Type 2.

What is different: the immune system does NOT attack the beta cells, so it is not autoimmune like Type 1. It starts during pregnancy, mother and baby are monitored closely while she is pregnant, and blood sugar usually goes back to normal after the baby is born.

Why it matters here: a pregnant adult with gestational diabetes is not a kid with Type 1. Different cause, different timing, different care, so please do not mix them up.

Why gestational diabetes is easier than Type 1

In gestational diabetes the key still exists, the pancreas still makes insulin (in fact it makes more during pregnancy), but placenta hormones make that key difficult to turn. In Type 1 there is no key at all: the beta cells are destroyed, so insulin must come from outside the body every day, for life.

Gestational diabetes is also temporary, when the baby and placenta are delivered the cause goes away and blood sugar usually returns to normal. That is why the effort is lower: often food choices, activity and blood-sugar checks for a few months, though some people need insulin. Type 1 never pauses and does not go away.

Gestational in one line: the key is difficult to turn, placenta hormones make it stiff, and it usually ends after the baby is born.

At a glance

Healthy: key turns easily, door opens. Type 2: key turns halfway, then gets stuck. Type 1: no key at all, external insulin needed. Gestational: key is difficult to turn.

Same word, diabetes, four very different jobs.

Type Is insulin made? Does the key work? What starts it? Effort to manage, and how disruptive it is
Healthy Yes Key turns easily, door opens – None. Automatic, the pancreas does it all. No counting, no monitoring, no insulin.
Gestational Yes Key is difficult to turn, placenta hormones Placenta hormones in pregnancy Low to medium. Often managed with diet, activity and blood-sugar checks during pregnancy; some need insulin. Usually ends after birth.
Type 2 Yes, at first Key turns halfway, then gets stuck Insulin resistance (metabolic) Medium to high. Lifelong, but often managed at first with food, activity and pills. Some people later need injections or insulin.
Type 1 Little or none No key at all, external insulin needed (pump or injections) Autoimmune attack on beta cells Hardest, highest. Lifelong and extremely disruptive: insulin every day by pump or injections, CGM monitoring 24/7, carb counting at every meal, and daily ups and downs.

Understanding the difference helps eliminate stigma and ensures kids with Type 1 get the exact medical support and understanding they need at school and sports. Same word, diabetes, but different causes, so the support has to fit the condition.

Food & Carb Counting November 2026

Top Foods and Carb Counting

Counting carbs is how I figure out my food. These are my handout posters — the foods I reach for, the ones I count carefully, and the treats I plan for. My rule is simple: count it, pair it with protein and vegetables, and check your CGM after.

Values marked ~ are calculated estimates for a typical serving, not printed on the poster — check your own care plan.

No-Carb — About 0g

About 0g on the poster means these are foods Aviva usually doesn’t count, but they aren’t literally all zero. Real values per serving are below.

  • Eggs1 Large~1g
  • Cheese1 oz~1g
  • Chicken3 oz0g
  • Fish3 oz0g
  • Cucumber1 Cup~4g
  • Water1 Glass0g
  • Sparkling Ice1 Can0g
  • Sugar Free Jellos1 Cup0g
  • Hot Dog1~2g
  • Turkey Slices2 oz~1g
  • Beef3 oz0g
  • Bacon2 Slices~0g
  • Spinach1 Cup~1g
  • Lettuce with Ranch1 cup with 2 Tbsp ranch~2g
  • Mushrooms1 Cup~2g
  • Olives10~1g
  • Celery Sticks1 Cup~3g
  • Dill Pickles1 Pickle~1g

If I’m not low and I don’t have activity coming up, I drink this instead: water, Sparkling Ice, coconut milk, soymilk, or Fairlife milk.

If you drink it, count it — 1 Large Boba = 110g, about 2 meals of carbs.
